title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Unsolicited Opinions

During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
raw_summary: METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post ), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff). That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago. Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report). If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon. And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can . For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration. I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this? Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have. This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here , here ), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months. We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs. If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products? Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs? Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research? Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us. To some extent, our work is probably less accelerated by AI than Anthropic capabilities research is. I think most of our empirical research is similarly well-suited to AI speedup to most published ML capabilities research. Maybe Anthropic capabilities research is particularly well suited to AI speedup compared to most ML research? Some of the pretraining work may rely more on the AI's strengths. This could be the case if, for example, a big blocker on running experiments on new architectures is implementing them efficiently. One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work. Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed? A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to. And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement? There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows. Whatever the case is, I feel like we are imminently going to learn a lot about how feasible it is to accelerate AI safety research using AI labor. If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong. See also AI speeds up 3rd party safety researchers by ~1.6x (via self-reports) Discuss

title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
raw_summary: Earlier this week,  Anthropic stated in their S1  that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In  their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems.  From my reading of  their report  and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the  Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are  still  improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than  the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including  the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Importantly,  if AI   is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by  much  more than that. The rest of the post: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai Tweet thread: https://x.com/ajeya_cotra/status/2118802809814708533 Discuss

title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
raw_summary: I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later. Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll probably be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate. Take-off Speed from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me : Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.) At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall). Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: "An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips" How should we characterise progress up until now? Eliezer recently wrote : If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience. Tom Davidson responded : If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that. For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”. “Bumpy” intelligence explosions Forethought defines an additional scenario . For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs. (Diagram note: the types of intelligence explosion will be explained in the next section) In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology ) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Richard Ngo also expects jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts” (nonetheless he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”): Getting into the weeds Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible. Types of “Intelligence Explosion”: Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops : Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion: software only recursive self-improvement AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design, full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips. The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff. Projecting trends into the future: Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly , when we should be thinking exponentially ” This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view. In contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish): He also has a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward): Connor Leahry writes : “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty. Are we experiencing RSI? Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) with the following: “our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI” ( click for their definition ). Jack Clarke had previously commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027” Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”. ( Source ) METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue) Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns. I’ve attached a diagram showing self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others. Key crux: to what extent do benchmark scores correspond to real world capabilities? Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier. Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI. I found the Anthropic self-improveme…

title: Positive and Negative AI Futures
raw_summary: I'm continuing to share some notes I created for myself to use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I really like using Ilya: the AI scientist shaping the world as a way of engaging students at the start of a course. The video primarily focuses on the way that AI could go wrong, however, it also starts with “Now, AI is a great thing…”, so it naturally leads to a discussion of positive and negative futures. Positive Futures: One obvious resource on positive futures Foresight Institute’s Existential Hope website. I’ve browsed their content in the past, some of it is kind of interesting, but honestly, I found view it as mostly pretty mid. They also run a fellowship which has an existential hope stream: They recently released The AI future nobody is showing you , which resulted in a wide range of reactions on Twitter. I think this is worth commenting on as it illustrates the challenges with attempting to produce a positive vision. Honestly, I’ve become quite pessimistic here: the gap between what different groups in society want may simply be too wide for it to be possible to find a positive vision that unites society: Steven Pinker was positive: “A more plausible vision, in my view, than either Utopia or doom.” Nikola Jurkovic was in the middle: “I admire the effort… but sadly this story falls into the common narrative trap of just assuming that AGI won’t actually be deployed widely.” @HellenicVibes hated it: “Wow how exciting to have a thousand years under the boot of ‘community leaders,’ ‘impacted minorities,’ and ‘AI auditors!’ I would literally rather be turned into paperclips.” Would it matter if there doesn’t exist a unifying positive vision? What’s wrong with different people having different visions of a positive future? Well, I wouldn’t say anything is wrong with people having different visions per se, but I suspect it makes navigating the path forward much harder, even if everyone broadly agrees that certain outcomes would be bad. Whilst Dario wrote Machines of Loving Grace that argued most people were under-estimating the update he has also argued that the public’s current negative perception of AI is unlikely to shift in response to messaging (“a glitzy marketing campaign”). He argues that it is fundamentally a matter of trust with the causes going back decades. What matters is not talking about curing cancer, but “actually curing cancer” or other diseases. Forethought has a series on Better Futures which argues that Flourishing is currently underrated relative to surviving on the basis of scale and neglectedness. I think the series should actually be called “Best Futures” as that’s his true focus, largely as a result of his (mostly) risk-neutral stance. There is also a course , though “Better Futures work” is something of a misnomer as that implies more distinctness from standard x-risk/catastrophic risk work than this is given that the Better Futures perspective only makes most such work more important on the margin. Negative Futures: It’s worth remembering that the Ilya video started with him saying, “Now, AI is a great thing…” Of course, by the time you get to the end of the video and you’ve heard all the ways this can go wrong, it’s very easy to forget that he said that and reduce him to a “doomer” when he actually believes that AI can be built safely . Dario has complained about this phenomenon too. In response to criticism that he should be “more of a positive advocate for his own industry”, Dario has claimed that his messaging has been “equally balanced between risks and benefits” and that people may be misunderstanding his views because negative clips are disproportionately likely to go viral. In There’s No Rule That Says We Make it , Rob Miles claims that people often have an implicit belief that humanity will “rise to the occasion” even if they wouldn’t actually endorse that statement. He suggests that this may derive from fiction, where we face challenges, but we almost always overcome then. He dismisses this fictional “evidence” as not real evidence. Whilst Rob is talking about existential risk, you could apply his argument more broadly to less severe risks as well. Intermediate Futures: Utopia or dystopia certainly aren’t the only two possibilities. There’s also the chance of an intermediate path and I wanted to mention it here for balance since most of the material in the course will stand in opposition to this perspective. One particularly prominent perspective in this vein is AI as a Normal Technology : “Transformative economic and societal impacts will be slow (on the timescale of decades)… We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the (foreseeable) future (their timescale here is vague, but they concede that their view “has failed and/or is no longer useful” if “strong AI” is “developed and deployed in the next decade”).” ( summary , guide , critique by AI Futures Project , common ground , viral music video critique “Thus Spoke Compute” ). Their project has three elements: A description of current AI A prediction about the foreseeable future A prescription about how we should respond (I have an instinctual reaction that using a single catchy phrase “AI as a Normal Technology” as a framework for answering three separate questions feels “too neat”. I acknowledge that simplicity is a virtue of an analytical framework andI admit this is a shallow objection, but nonetheless I do see this as a yellow flag). Additional detail: They have a three stage model of technological progress: invention, innovation and diffusion. They argue things will move slowly as further invention often requires additional learnings or data which can only come from iteratively diffusing/deploying the technology. They believe this process will take decades rather than years and that improvements in AI improvements can only accelerate this so much because the diffusion loop sets an overall “speed limit”. Key crux: can AI can contract the decades of diffusion by deploying itself or would the speed limit remain due to social factors, delays for testing models or repeated waits for data to be collected? Their view centres resilience over alignment (inherently brittle, requires models to have context which we might not want to give them) or non-proliferation (infeasible, brittle, increases correlated failures via market concentration, limits defensive use, not justified for speculative risks). “Attempting to make an AI model that cannot be misused is like trying to make a computer that cannot be used for bad things. Model-level safety controls will either be too restrictive (preventing beneficial uses) or will be ineffective against adversaries who can repurpose seemingly benign capabilities for harmful ends.” They also argued against focusing too much on catastrophic misalignment due to the risk being speculative (they argue that these probabilities are insufficiently grounded to form the basis of public policy). It’s natural to wonder where they stand post-Hugging Face. They have a post : They believe that many of their claims have “held up”, however they acknowledge making a few mistakes: “We did not pay sufficient attention to safety risks that arise during development and evaluation (as opposed to the widespread deployment of models)“: Lawrence Chan has argued AI models can be dangerous before public deployment . On that point Chernobyl was actually the result of a safety test (a post-deployment safety test, but still!) “We were too confident that companies would take basic control precautions”: They write: “our expectation was that existing legal liability, imperfect as it is, and the risk of brand damage would be a sufficient antidote to such organizational practices. We were wrong. This reinforces the need for policy interventions” “And underplayed the importance of jaggedness which led us to underestimate how quickly ca…

title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
raw_summary: TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata. A Theory of What? The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency). The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS ). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the environment they can exploit. For instance, if you switch the "cool" and "heat" outputs of a thermostat, it will not understand what has gone wrong and adapt its behavior. Animals and contemporary AIs are marginal cases (it's not obvious whether they should count). Given that agents are at the core of both the threat and the proposed solution, the theoretical foundation for ASI alignment requires a theory of agents. Now, concepts adjacent to "agent" have a considerable history of academic study, but different research communities approach the subject very differently—compare the frameworks used in decision theory (and, by extension, in game theory and economics), Hutter's " universal intelligence ", and reinforcement learning theory . It is therefore important to understand what the scope and level of abstraction of the theory of agents relevant for ASI alignment should be. To this end, I propose several desiderata. Descriptive The theory should be descriptive , i.e. applicable to all our main examples of agents. For any such example, the theory should ascribe specific preferences, beliefs, and any other alignment-relevant attributes to the agent [2] . These ascriptions should be grounded in the general philosophical soundness of the theory, not in domain knowledge about the specific examples; due to hypercomplexity , it is unlikely that domain knowledge will suffice [3] . In particular, if we imagine an alien civilization facing the AI alignment problem, or an AI agent facing the alignment problem for successor agents it wants to create, the theory should be about equally useful to them [4] . This means that agent theory should deconfuse us about philosophical questions pertaining to human preferences, such as, for example, the Caplan-Alexander debate on whether mental illness should be thought of as "unusual preferences". This doesn't mean that the answer to any particular question of this kind must be obvious from the theory, as it might come down to idiosyncratic nuances of the human brain. It does mean that if we also knew all pertinent facts about the physical world , we would be able to answer the question (or at least quantify the residual uncertainty), at least in principle. Actually inferring the answer from these facts might still be hard, just as explaining emergent physical phenomena can be hard even if all the relevant fundamental laws are known. On the other hand, descriptiveness doesn't require that concepts such as "human preferences" be perfectly unambiguous. It requires only that, to the extent they remain ambiguous, this ambiguity should not allow critical errors when Goodhart's Curse is accounted for. It is not obvious that these concepts can be made perfectly precise, but it is clear that the alignment problem is fundamentally normative (i.e. it is rooted in our preferring certain AI futures over other AI futures). When zooming in to a resolution at which our preferences are ill-defined, it becomes immaterial which choice to make, since our preferences are the only impetus for distinguishing these choices. Any imprecision that is inevitable is also tolerable. For example, imagine that Alice prefers to eat apples approximately 3 times as often as bananas, but there is no fully principled answer to the question "does Alice prefer to eat apples 2.99 times as often as bananas, or 3.01 times, or some number in the middle?" Then, it doesn't matter whether the AI aligned to Alice according to our theory will interpret her preference as 2.99 or 3.01—both are acceptable outcomes. In the mathematical formalism of the theory, this ambiguity might manifest as something like the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM) in Solomonoff induction. Different UTMs correspond to priors that differ merely by a multiplicative constant, but for particular pairs of UTMs this constant can be arbitrarily large. Then, a reasonable choice might be any machine that we would intuitively consider "simple" or "natural". This doesn't nail down a single UTM, but might come close enough for the differences not to matter in practice [5] . This situation is not fundamentally different from that of most concepts in science. For example, astrophysicists find no difficulty discussing the "center of mass of the Sun", even though strictly speaking it is ill-defined: the boundary of the Sun is fuzzy, particle positions are only well-defined down to the scale of their Compton wavelength, and even the notion of space itself becomes questionable in quantum gravity. Notably, a descriptive theory must neither underspecify nor overspecify what counts as an agent. For example, a theory that mandates that "agents" use stochastic gradient descent would probably exclude humans, and is hence overspecified. On the other hand, a theory that accepts anything that maximizes the expectation of some utility function as an "agent" would conclude that even a rock is an agent and would severely underspecify agent attributes (see e.g. Shah 2018 ). The correct theory should fall into neither extreme. Metareflective The theory should allow us to describe agents that learn, know, or use facts from agent theory itself. For example, it should be possible to: Describe an agent that plans to construct a successor agent but faces an alignment problem, and show how such an agent can overcome the alignment problem by learning and applying agent theory (all within the framework of agent theory itself). Describe an agent that identifies other agents in the universe and infers their preferences, beliefs, or other attributes. Describe an agent learning about a bound satisfied by a particular algorithm pertinent to agent theory, e.g. a statistical complexity bound. If a theory satisfies this desideratum, I say that it is metareflective [6] . There are several ways to see why metareflectiveness is important: If our theory is not metareflective, it might mean that it doesn't apply to humans, and hence it also isn't descriptive. The straightforward approach to solving alignment grounding is for the AI agent to infer the user's attributes by using (parts of) agent theory in its own reasoning. Metareflectiveness seems necessary to properly model recursive self-improvement . Recursive self-improvement is a factor that exacerbates AI risk, and hence the failure to model it might be indicative of a crucial gap in the theory. Classical learning theory is not metareflective: there is no standard way to describe how learning algorithms can …

title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Some general thoughts on advice I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another. In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?). Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear . People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less. (See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom : “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”) Some thoughts on frameworks People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few. I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions. Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them. The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown? Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made. This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice . Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes : “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.” Cruxes when attempting to predict the future: Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)? Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results? Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward). “AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”: I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course: If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence. Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper . These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence . Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AG…

title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
raw_summary: The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope , in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1 , 2 tl;dr I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name. 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition: In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me. Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior. 2. My headline claim Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose : they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident . The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations. (Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.) But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other. Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking): a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”, a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”. Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong , but they are pedagogically dicey —a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect. (And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.) We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names. Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue. …But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post? 3. (Backstory of this post) I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah ’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from? I think his position is something like (my words): For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense? That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.) Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat, [1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways. More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.) 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat 4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go? This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return. 4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021) : For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”). That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating , and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment! This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market. Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else.
