title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policie…

title: AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the E.U.’s New Rules
raw_summary: The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on OpenAI’s new textGrain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new E.U. law , show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether textGrain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated. AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next “tokens” (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li , coauthor of the textGrain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words. A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values—numbers produced by a mathematical process that influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says. What makes textGrain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and textGrain adjusts to that target. This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money.… In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.” Limits of AI Watermark Detection The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written. OpenAI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. In tests on psychology questions from the ELI5 database , which gathers questions and answers from the r/explainlikeimfive subreddit, the model detected watermarks in about 80 percent of 200-token text ( approximately 150 words ) compared to 95 percent of 400-token text (approximately 300 words). Li says this is a “basic limitation” of text-watermarking technologies and would be complicated to solve. Short passages may not contain enough watermark evidence for reliable detection, even with additional computation, he adds, while longer passages generally provide more. Editing also weakens the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing just 10 percent of words with synonyms reduced detection from 92 percent to 66 percent; replacing up to 25 percent cut the detection rate to 17 percent, according to OpenAI. Because the watermark depends on preceding tokens, changing one word can disrupt the signal at several positions, Li says. OpenAI says watermarking alone is not enough to determine whether content is AI-generated. TextGrain will “complement” other provenance tools, such as content credentials in the metadata and SynthID watermarks developed by Google DeepMind for images and audio outputs. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. E.U. AI Act Transparency Obligations The transparency obligations in Article 50 of the E.U. AI Act went into effect on 2 August. The law requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, images, video, or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Technical solutions must be “effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible,” according to the law. The E.U.’s Code of Practice offers a voluntary way for providers to show how they will be compliant. This code does not require watermarks on outputs shorter than 200 tokens. Thomas Souverain , a postdoctoral fellow on AI Ethics at the Institute of Advanced Education, in Paris, says the legislation is open to interpretation. Souverain says that the early methodology behind textGrain seems reliable and could work better than its competitors at identifying AI-generated text. OpenAI says textGrain matched or outperformed Google’s SynthID Text in its own tests, but those results have not been independently verified. Until independent researchers can test it, and while the AI Act’s criteria still lack measurable thresholds, it is too early to say whether textGrain meets legal requirements. “We only have a technical study…there hasn’t been a peer-reviewed academic article, and we don’t [yet] have access to a precise protocol [for textGrain],” Souverain says. OpenAI is working with a limited group of researchers that includes John Thickstun , an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, and researchers at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies (KInIT) in Bratislava, Slovakia. Thickstun and Dominik Macko , a senior researcher at KInIT, says they had only just gained access and had not yet begun evaluating the system. Macko says his team plans to test textGrain’s “robustness” across different subject areas, languages, and text lengths. If textGrain is eventually found to not meet the E.U.’s requirements, Souverain says, OpenAI could face a fine of up to 7 percent of its annual income. Souverain also calls on OpenAI to make textGrain open-source so that researchers not on their team can “identify all the faults, paraphrases and possible translation faults” of the model by trying to break it. “I see the corporate interest, if there is a big flaw detected, a big weakness, [that] it is detected in the background,” he said. “But I would like to see an even more open phase, such as today with SynthID, [where] we have access to the methods.”

title: How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses
raw_summary: The first time Mutembei Kariuki thought about how AI models could work in Kenya, his home country, was in 2019. He was attending a conference at the University of Tokyo on the future of AI, and kept hearing about how this technology was going to transform the world. “But nobody mentioned Africa at all,” he says. Even then—before AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic had launched their chatbots to the public—Kariuki could see significant obstacles to AI adoption in Africa. Internet access was slow and unequal, computing resources for training models were scarce, and there was little high-quality, structured training data. Most people, meanwhile, reached the internet through outdated, low-memory cellphones rather than computers or high-end phones. Together with cofounders Jude Mwenda and Stephanie Njerenga , Kariuki created Fastagger , a startup that builds AI models that can run offline and on low-power cellphones. Its first big product, Auni, is a business-intelligence assistant that launched in 2024; it got a big push when it was integrated into the business app of M-Pesa , Kenya’s largest mobile money service. Since then, about 6,000 businesses have signed up. Auni helps small and medium businesses like barbershops, restaurants, and small manufacturers analyze their transaction data and gives them marketing recommendations. Peter Chege, owner of a salon and barbershop in Nairobi, started using Auni last year. Before that, he recorded all his sales on paper. “We were not able to translate that information into a graph,” he says. Now, the app helps him identify his busiest days and hours, as well as his loyal customers. If a regular customer stops coming, for example, he can send a personalized message encouraging them to return. Fastagger is part of an emerging effort to build AI around the technological realities of users in developing economies, rather than adapting products designed for wealthier markets. In Fastagger’s case, that meant finding a way to make their models work despite inexpensive phones, unreliable internet connections, and business records that may consist of little more than mobile-money transactions. Designing AI for Kenya’s Small Businesses Before developing Auni, Kariuki and his cofounders started by tackling the problem of data availability for AI training. They asked themselves: “How do we get Africa to catch up fast? How do we create training data fast enough, and then how do we actually get it into people’s hands fast enough?” Mutembei Kariuki cofounded Fastagger to develop AI systems that can run offline and on basic phones. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft They decided to focus on mobile phones, and specifically on mobile money apps. With more than 80 percent of Kenya’s adults using them, they offer a rich source of data. One of Fastagger’s first steps was to adapt an open-source optical character recognition (OCR) model to read financial statements produced by mobile money apps. Existing models struggled with the low quality of the PDFs, which had unfamiliar formatting and sometimes contained stamps and errors. And because Fastagger’s prospective users often had unreliable internet connections, they made sure that key steps, like organizing the extracted data into tables, could run on-device. Once they had a model that could process these documents, they began exploring how that structured financial data could help businesses. They spent entire days watching small-business owners work and interact with their customers. One challenge quickly became clear: Owners had little time or resources to think beyond day-to-day operations. “They are standing up the whole day cutting hair,” Kariuki says of salon owners, who are now among Auni’s main users. “You have to think about that dynamic of the user journey, and how they live, and what will be going on in the background.” The Fastagger app helps salon owner Peter Chege better manage his time and keep track of loyal customers. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft For Chege, one of Auni’s biggest benefits was helping him manage his time. A simple chart showed him that mornings were his slowest hours, so he realized that he could run errands then or keep fewer barbers in the shop until around 1 p.m., when business picked up. The founders also saw how much time businesses spent on manual processes and how automation could simplify those tasks. At a fish restaurant in Nairobi, for example, identifying loyal customers to offer them discounts required going through SMS sales receipts one by one, a tedious task that rendered client-retention marketing impractical. Now, with the help of Auni, the restaurant identifies its top customers automatically and offers them discounts. Some of Auni’s functions—such as reading sales statements, analyzing data, and visualizing results—can happen offline on low-cost phones, without making cloud queries. These functions involve both AI tools and conventional software; for example, standard OCR software extracts the text and a small neural network identifies how each document is structured. More detailed analyses and answering questions about the data, however, require an internet connection. Daniel Björkegren , an economist at Columbia University who studies AI’s implications for developing economies, says sub-Saharan Africa’s prevalence of basic phones rather than smartphones and computers could open the door to different kinds of AI use. “The history of technology should suggest that this is not going to be people running Claude Code or Codex on their laptop,” he says. “You will have people like that, but for much of the population, we’re going to have to figure out different usage modalities.” How Local Needs Are Shaping AI Despite Auni’s integration into M-Pesa, Fastagger remains a small startup. It has received support from Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia accelerator programs, but still has just three employees: Kariuki, Mwenda, and Njerenga, the original founders. Currently, they’re working on adding agents to Auni that could automatically implement marketing actions for business owners. Fastagger has also developed a workforce management tool for Kenya’s security companies, which employ hundreds of thousands of people. Security guards often work in remote locations without reliable internet and use low-end phones. Fastagger’s AI agent communicates with them via SMS to track their routes, detects anomalies, and generates actionable alerts for operations teams. Fastagger isn’t alone in tailoring AI models for the usage conditions in emerging economies. Other examples include an app for rural schools without internet in Chile ; a medical triage chatbot for rural patients in India , and translation models for African languages that run on basic phones . Such innovations, which emerge from constraints, could help democratize access to AI. But that doesn’t mean the constraints themselves disappear or stop limiting development. While Björkegren sees great potential in systems built for populations that have been poorly served by Silicon Valley, he believes there’s a risk in establishing too clear a division between small models designed for emerging economies and increasingly large, powerful models for wealthier regions. “I am worried that that could lead to a bifurcation,” he says. “We need to enable a large menu of different options and really make sure that we have access and then see what works.”

title: The Race to Build a “Find My” for AI Chips
raw_summary: In a bid to limit China’s AI capabilities, the United States imposed restrictions in 2022 on the export of certain advanced chips to China. But throughout the AI boom those chips have kept turning up in China anyway . On 1 October 2026, the U.S. arrested a man on charges of sending over $300 million worth of GPU-equipped servers to China using paperwork intended for shipments to Malaysia and Singapore . As chip smuggling and diversion continues, the United States is learning that the more it tries to limit the motion of its AI chips, the harder they are to precisely locate . To help curb the issue, the country is turning to location verification. Last March, the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee passed a bill requiring location verification for advanced AI chips. Ahead of the U.S.-China summit in late September, legislators called for a floor vote on that and related bills. If such a requirement were to pass, how would chipmakers comply? They could build tamper-proof root of trust hardware, implement cryptographic signing and transmission, or possibly even fingerprint individual chips. These strategies could function as a way to keep track of where AI chips actually are in the world, much like how the popular “Find My” feature can locate misplaced Apple devices. Pings that pinpoint positions Location verification can take different forms, such as geolocation mechanisms, inventory management tools, mail-in inspections, and video inspections. A combination of approaches, such as ping-based location verification (PLV) supplemented by physical inspections, would be a feasible and robust approach, say the authors of a September Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) report on chip location tracking. To deduce an AI chip’s location, PLV measures the time it takes for a ping to travel from the chip to multiple trusted “landmark” servers around the world and back. Kyle Miller , a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, says that for new AI chips, manufacturers could integrate PLV functionality into the hardware itself, while a firmware update could be applied to chips already in circulation. Not all AI chips should be tracked, the researchers note. “The priority should be for the highest-end data center chips—the cream of the crop in high-end data center GPUs,” says Jacob Feldgoise , a senior data research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report. A similar initiative involves transmitting encrypted “ sovereignty certificates .” These certificates act as “cryptographic credentials that provide verifiable, unforgeable proof of the physical location of a computing device, such as a CPU or GPU, at a specific point in time,” per the draft specification published by secure computing firm Lucid Computing . “If you can use a private key that exists on a particular chip, and you can sign a message with that cryptographic key, and then that message is received by a so-called landmark server, then you can send a couple of those messages and time those messages. A lot of modern chips come with trusted execution environments that support a hardware root of trust where you can sign these messages,” says Kristian Rönn , CEO and cofounder of Lucid Computing. “You get a radius of where the chip has to be.” PLV could have some effect on chip smugglers, Miller says. “They know if they turn this chip on, it’s going to start pinging these landmark servers. That could deter some smuggling.” And when the system flags a chip as residing in a nonintended location, “the PLV data gives you a better sense of when and where it was moved,” he adds. However, ping-based location verification can only uncover diversion after it has happened. It can’t track offline chips that are in storage, in transit, or have yet to be activated. And when a chip fails to respond to a ping request, the system won’t know whether it’s due to a valid reason or nefarious causes. This is where physical inspections come in. “You need to do that follow-on investigative work. You need to physically go to these data centers and do those physical audits as well. Essentially, [PLV] generates leads, and you track down those leads,” says Miller. A PLV system involves sending signals from a chip to and from trusted servers and measuring the travel time. Source image: CSET A “lie detector” for data centers Despite the safeguards around ping-based location verification, the methodology remains vulnerable to particular attacks. If adversaries gain physical access to a chip, for example, they could prevent it from sending signals, or they could extract cryptographic keys and spoof a signal from the intended location. To fight that, some security researchers are exploring hardware fingerprints instead of cryptographic keys. One study demonstrated a proof-of-concept GPU fingerprinting function that produced unique fingerprints for Nvidia H200 GPUs based on their manufacturing variations and random numbers as seeds. “You want to support other types of fingerprinting because not all chips have a hardware root of trust. You might want to use some statistical fingerprinting to know that the chip is what it’s supposed to be,” Rönn says. “It also requires good physical security around the chips, such as tamper-proofing. Over time, you ideally want to have more defense in depth.” Additionally, the CSET report warns that PLV is costly. And if China achieves the ability to craft its own advanced AI chips, “then tracking the export of U.S. chips is less of a strategic priority,” says Miller. Hanna Dohmen , a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, points to other gaps in the U.S. export control regime. “Currently, Chinese companies are legally able to remotely access AI chips abroad through cloud service providers,” she says. These advanced AI chips might be installed in data centers across Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, which are increasingly serving Chinese firms . Whether or not a “Find My” for AI chips becomes a regulatory requirement, Feldgoise envisions tighter conditions for the export of advanced AI chips. “This is based on the increasing importance of compute to national and economic security,” he says. “The chips that generate compute are being seen as a strategic resource, so I would be unsurprised if the due diligence requirements on these devices increase as time passes.” Rönn views sovereignty certificates as essential tools in the future, likening it to a “lie detector” for data centers that answer the “where, how, what, and who questions for us to know that they comply with a basic standard of security when it comes to AI systems.”

title: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
raw_summary: The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza , it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing. A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse. In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out. “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are. Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona. Václav Široký During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study . In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona. And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that. A Mathematician’s Path to Solar Eclipse Photography Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas , an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one. An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field. Miloslav Druckmüller He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens . All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse. He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.” A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain. Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view. What Solar Eclipses Reveal About the Corona The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot : about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core. To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere. That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface. Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal , a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography. The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team. How Eclipse Images Sparked a Scientific Partnership When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field. It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive. Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habba…

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
raw_summary: AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026 Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August , September , and October . November 2026 Summary In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July. OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one . OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December. More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on. Decision models account for 26% of all requests Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive. Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model. They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model. Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend. Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models. Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did. This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively. Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%. New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%. Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July. A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps: A voice model turns the user’s speech into text A language model writes the reply Another voice model reads the reply back to the user Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled. Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped. For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both. Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54. Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five. Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI. But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets. On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period. Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten. Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models. Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab. Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens. AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one. Also in October’s data Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two. Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten. OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0. About this data This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026. A few notes on measurement: Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month. Decision models are the models classified as d…

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
raw_summary: The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later. Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on. Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens: Streams keep pace with AI output In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second. Fewer HTTP requests for event writes Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery. Get started Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide , since v5 is a major release. Read more

title: Build disk space on Vercel increased to 64 GB
raw_summary: Disk space for Vercel builds has increased from 32 GB to 64 GB on Basic and Standard machines, matching the capacity already available on Enhanced and Turbo. The additional space provides more room for the packages your project uses and the files generated during a build, reducing the risk of running out of disk space. The change applies automatically across all plans and build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration changes required. Learn more in the build machine documentation . Read more

title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
raw_summary: Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB. The registry works with standard workflows like docker push , docker pull , and docker tag , and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly. Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions . The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images. Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion. See the documentation for the full setup. Read more

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
raw_summary: Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway . Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max , with high as the API default. Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2. To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks . Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway , and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request. Call it through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name: This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format. To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more

title: Muse Ember now available on AI Gateway

title: Gaining (and losing) currency: a global database of currencies, 1850-2026
raw_summary: Over the past two centuries, officially issued currencies have become firmly en trenched as a nearly universal institution in economies around the world. But the path to this arrangement has not been smooth: currencies have come and gone, in line with political changes, periods of hyperinflation or currency reforms and, in some cases, entry into currency unions.

title: Scenarios for future banking: implications for profitability, liquidity and solvency
raw_summary: Who will perform banking’s core functions a decade from now, and how will risks and profitability evolve? Our framework structures expert judgement rather than forecasts.

title: Prewar US business cycles under uncertainty: reconstructing quarterly GDP before 1947
raw_summary: Official quarterly US GDP estimates begin in 1947; earlier quarterly histories must be reconstructed using annual benchmarks and historical indicators. To investigate uncertainty in these reconstructions, this paper systematically compares specifications drawn from the literature for reconstructing quarterly GDP during 1919–1946. The comparison evaluates predictions on concealed postwar quarters and separates variation across specifications from coefficient uncertainty within a model.

title: Smile dynamics and rough volatility
raw_summary: The joint spot-smile dynamics is analysed through the skew stickiness ratio lens

title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
raw_summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
raw_summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
raw_summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
raw_summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
raw_summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

title: FEDS Paper: Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges
raw_summary: Krzysztof Wozniak Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

title: FEDS Paper: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
raw_summary: Aditya Aladangady , Ricardo Duque Gabriel , and Carlo Wix We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.

title: Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights
raw_summary: Highlights from UIUC’s 2026 ASKS Fall Symposium. On September 24–25, academic researchers, enterprise scientists and leaders gathered at the Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) for the ASKS Fall Symposium. The event marked a major milestone in the partnership between Capital One and the University of Illinois through the Capital One Center for Generative AI Safety, Knowledge Systems and Cybersecurity (ASKS). Designed to advance the safety, reliability and security of generative AI models, the symposium featured keynotes, research readouts, panel debates and a hands-on AI red-teaming workshop. From models to agents: Navigating the age of action The symposium kicked off with opening remarks and a fireside chat titled “From models to agents: rethinking AI research, safety, and cybersecurity in the age of action.” Moderated by ASKS Co-Director Heng Ji, the session featured Prem Natarajan, chief scientist and chief enterprise AI officer at Capital One, alongside Nancy Amato, director of the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. The discussion framed the fundamental transition taking place across the AI landscape: moving away from models that merely generate text to autonomous agentic AI-systems that can set goals, execute code, operate tools and take multistep actions. Natarajan highlighted Capital One’s “destination-back” scientific approach, emphasizing that in highly regulated spaces like financial services, autonomous agency requires rigorous safety mechanisms. As AI stops just “talking” and starts “acting,” industry-academic partnerships like ASKS become essential to build new sandboxing, auditing and accountability frameworks. Panel spotlight: Word models vs. world models One of the highlights of the day was a panel exploring the fundamental limits of current large language models: “ Word models vs. world models: Do LLMs understand the world-or just describe it? ” Moderated by Heng Ji, the panel brought together UIUC faculty members Gang Wang, Julia Hockenmaier, Chengxiang Zhai and Katie Driggs-Campbell alongside Capital One AI leaders Sambit Sahu and Yue (Rex) Wu. The panelists debated whether modern foundation models genuinely comprehend real-world dynamics or simply replicate statistical language patterns. The consensus pointed toward a need for multimodal visual grounding, physical intelligence and trace-aware reasoning to move models from passive text descriptions to true situation understanding. Pioneering research readouts Throughout the symposium, awarded faculty members and doctoral fellows presented breakthrough findings from ASKS-funded research projects spanning safety, code reasoning and cybersecurity: LLM reasoning and faithfulness: Hao Peng presented work on advancing reasoning faithfulness without explicit rewards, while Talia Ringer’s team introduced TrACE-Contrast for faithful code reasoning. Yuxiong Wang presented work on building safe and trustworthy LLM-based agents by addressing key challenges in evaluation, privacy preservation and multi-agent coordination. Guaranteed safety for agentic AI: Sasa Misailovic detailed SafeAgency , a framework designed to guarantee safety in agentic workflows, complemented by Katherine Driggs-Campbell’s analysis of failures in agentic systems. Security and cybersecurity benchmarks: Bo Li’s team showcased Sentinel Agent for secure agentic architectures, Varun Chandrasekaran’s team presented insights into pragmatic LLM jailbreaking and Daniel Kang introduced CVE-Bench++ , a benchmark for evaluating AI agents in cybersecurity contexts. Keynote on code generation safety: ASKS Director Gang Wang delivered a keynote on automated red-teaming and reasoning to secure code generation models. Doctoral fellow spotlights: Emerging researchers Hyeonjeong Ha, Jeonghwan Kim, Yizhuo Chen, Cheng Qian and Chenyuan Yang presented research on perceptual grounding, data sanitization and physical intelligence. The afternoon program highlighted Capital One’s research initiatives during a session chaired by Sambit Sahu, featuring lightning talks by senior research directors Kartik Balasubramaniam, Genta Winata and Stephen Rawls on scalable AI foundations and system architecture. Red-teaming workshop On the second day of the event, domain specialists convened for a smaller, more intimate AI red-teaming workshop. Alexandre Day (Capital One), Sriram Venkatapathy (Capital One), Varun Chandrasekaran (UIUC) and Gang Wang (UIUC) organized technical talks and working group sessions across three primary focus areas: Novel and diversity-driven red-teaming: Led by Capital One’s Sriram Venkatapathy, the session examined how financial AI systems must adhere to strict multilayered policy frameworks-spanning federal regulations (e.g., FCRA, UDAP), enterprise governance and application-specific constraints. Discussions highlighted that evaluating enterprise safety requires detecting policy omissions (such as missing mandatory disclosures or consent prompts) as well as defending against strategy-conditioned jailbreaks, chain-of-thought forgery and loopholes in complex policy specifications. Red-teaming multi-agent systems: Led by Gang Wang, this track focused on security vulnerabilities unique to multi-agent architectures. Researchers analyzed risks such as indirect prompt injection across workspace topologies, lateral attack propagation between trusted agents, execution-level coordination failures (e.g., data races and deadlocks) and communication-layer enforcement via protocols like NLIP. Evaluation of red-teaming and LLM judges: Led by Rikhiya Ghosh, participants tackled the open challenges of scientifically evaluating safety across long-horizon, multiturn interactions. The group audited LLM-as-a-judge frameworks using semantic factorization (MoE judges), probed reasoning traces for stealthy deception and monitorability failures and explored methods to prevent benchmark contamination through dynamic case generation. Fostering the frontier of talent and research The partnership between Capital One and UIUC continues to drive technical innovation while training the next generation of scientific talent. Highlighting joint breakthroughs like MEMGUARD-a defense mechanism preventing memory contamination in LLMs-the ASKS Center demonstrates the power of combining academic exploration with industrial scale. Capital One looks forward to continuing this strategic collaboration, advancing research in agentic AI and building systems that remain secure, trustworthy and beneficial at scale. Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights was originally published in Capital One Tech on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
